pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You call cancel() on a context and a worker goroutine three function calls away stops. Explain the mechanism end to end — what actually travels from cancel() to that goroutine?
expected_points: cancel closes the context's Done channel, and the Done of every context derived from it
a closed channel unblocks every receiver — close is a one-to-many broadcast
the worker only stops because it selects on ctx.Done(); cancellation is cooperative, nothing kills goroutines
the worker returns ctx.Err() so callers learn why it stopped

questions.prompt: When would you reach for WithDeadline instead of WithTimeout? And why does every With* call come with a defer cancel() on the next line, even when the operation succeeds?
expected_points: WithTimeout is WithDeadline sugar: relative budget vs absolute instant
an absolute deadline propagates intact across hops; re-deriving a relative timeout at each hop silently extends the budget
cancel releases the deadline timer and unlinks the context from its parent's tree
goroutines blocked on that Done stay blocked until cancel; deferring covers every return path, and calling it after success is the point, not an error

questions.prompt: Why does every context-aware function take ctx as its first parameter instead of the containing struct holding one context for all its methods?
expected_points: a context's lifetime is one call tree; a struct's lifetime spans many calls or requests
a stored context couples unrelated requests — one caller's cancellation kills the others
explicit passing keeps cancellation flow visible at every call site
convention: first parameter, named ctx; pass context.Background() rather than nil

questions.prompt: A teammate passes the database handle to lower layers via context.WithValue "to keep signatures clean". What do you tell them — what does Value exist for, and how do you decide what belongs there?
expected_points: Value carries request-scoped metadata riding alongside the call: request ID, trace span, authenticated user
the test: the function must still do its job if the value is absent — metadata yes, dependencies and parameters no
dependencies through Value are invisible and untyped: the compiler can't check them
keys should be unexported types with typed accessors so other packages cannot collide

questions.prompt: A call into a slow service returns an error. How do you tell whether the budget ran out or someone gave up on purpose, and why should your code react differently to each?
expected_points: ctx.Err() is one of two sentinels: context.DeadlineExceeded (clock ran out) vs context.Canceled (deliberate cancel)
compare with errors.Is, never ==, because layers wrap errors with %w
deadline exceeded is transient — retrying with a fresh budget can work
canceled is a decision — retrying wastes work or duplicates side effects

questions.prompt: A worker selects on ctx.Done() while receiving jobs, then sends each result with a plain results <- r. Its consumer gets canceled and stops reading. What happens to the worker, and why does no test without a timeout ever catch it?
expected_points: the unguarded send blocks forever once nobody drains results — a goroutine leak
cancellation must guard every blocking operation, sends included, via a second select
the race detector stays silent: nothing races, the goroutine just never ends

questions.prompt: context.Background().Done() returns a nil channel. Why does a select with a case <-ctx.Done() still behave correctly when handed Background?
expected_points: receiving from a nil channel blocks forever
in a select, that case simply never becomes ready, so the other cases proceed
Background is never canceled, so 'never ready' is exactly the right semantics
